To this dynamic theory Adams added a Law of Acceleration: coal-output doubling every decade, force compounding upon force, the human meteor drawn ever faster toward a perihelion at which the mind itself would have to leap into a new equilibrium or be dissipated.

NUNC AGE (1905)

Nearly forty years had passed since the ex-private secretary landed at New York with his father, when they saw American society as a long caravan stretching out towards the plains. As he came up the bay again, November 5, 1904, he found the approach more striking than ever—wonderful, unlike anything man had ever seen, and like nothing he had ever much cared to see. Power seemed to have outgrown its servitude and to have asserted its freedom. The cylinder had exploded, and thrown great masses of stone and steam against the sky. The city had the air and movement of hysteria; all New York was demanding new men, and the new forces, condensed into corporations, demanded a new type of man—with ten times the endurance, energy, will and mind of the old. A traveller in the highways of history looked out on the turmoil of Fifth Avenue, and felt himself in Rome, under Diocletian. The two-thousand-years failure of Christianity roared upward from Broadway, and no Constantine the Great was in sight.

He went on to Washington, where Roosevelt was training Constantines and battling Trusts. With the Battle of Trusts a student of mechanics felt entire sympathy, as a measure of motion. The new American must be either the child of the new forces or a chance sport of nature. If the acceleration were to continue at its rate since 1800, the mathematician of 1950 should be able to plot the past and future orbit of the human race as accurately as that of the November meteoroids. Therefore dispute was idle, discussion futile, and silence the mark of sense.

Arriving November 14, Adams saw at a glance that Hay must have rest. His formula for Russian inertia proved exasperatingly correct: Russia should have negotiated instantly on the fall of Port Arthur, but had not the energy. The delay measured precisely the time Hay had to spare. The close of the Session left Hay barely strength to crawl on board ship, March 18; at sea he revived. He nourished no illusions; he was convinced he should never return to his work. In eight years of office he had solved nearly every old problem of American statesmanship, and brought the great Atlantic powers into a working system. For the first time in fifteen hundred years a true Roman *pax* was in sight.

After Nervi and Nauheim, Hay came on to Paris, having lost strength. In their last talk before he started for Liverpool, the remonstrance was: "You must hold out for the peace negotiations."

"I've not time!" he replied.

"You'll need little time!" was the rejoinder.

Each was correct.

A few weeks afterwards, one warm evening in early July, as Adams was strolling down to dine under the trees at Armenonville, he learned that Hay was dead. "The rest is silence!" The few familiar words served Shakespeare, and, as yet, no one has said more. It was only the quiet summons to follow—the assent to dismissal. It was time to go. The three friends had begun life together, and the last had no motive to carry it on. Perhaps some day—say 1938, their centenary—they might be allowed to return together for a holiday, and find a world that sensitive and timid natures could regard without a shudder.

THE END
